1.pericope_label: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the Lord. Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem... whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the Lord

schools.summary: Delitzsch accounts for the psalm's place in the collection and notes the missing Davidic ascription in the chief Greek copies; Ellicott corrects the tense of the second verse and canvasses three senses of 'compact together'.
Gill spiritualises the gates and the city into the church and the New Jerusalem; Calvin grounds the joy in the settling of the ark at last and in the people's unanimous consent to the oracle.
Clarke reads the psalm as the thanksgiving of captives returning under the edict of Cyrus; Wesley identifies the testimony with the ark and its tables.
Henry turns 'let us go' into a rule of mutual encouragement in public worship; Spurgeon makes the whole gladness turn on that same plural.
Augustine reads the degrees as ascents and the city as the eternal Jerusalem, where the angels are fellow-citizens and we are wanderers summoned on by companions who have already seen her.

debates.question: When and by whom was the psalm written?

positions.summary: By David, on the settling of the ark at Zion. Jebb's internal evidence — the fond mention of Jerusalem, the thrones of David's house, the recurrence of peace — outweighs the wordplay that might argue a later date.
By the returning captives after the edict of Cyrus, whose first thanksgiving was for permission to return to the ordinances.
Unsettled: the Davidic ascription is missing from the chief Greek copies, and the psalm reads as a visitor's benediction remembered after a feast.

debates.question: What does 'builded as a city that is compact together' mean?

positions.summary: The fabric: the upper and lower city joined, the houses contiguous rather than straggling, every part strengthening the whole — and so the church, compact when its members are united in affection.

Three readings are possible — the rebuilding of parts disconnected in the destruction, a countryman's astonishment at his first compact city, or, best, the Greek taking the word as a noun meaning union, so that she is the rallying point of the tribes.
The union is of the tribes, who came together there at the three great feasts and were still distinguished as twelve after the Exile.

debates.question: What is the tense and force of 'Our feet shall stand'?

positions.summary: Not future but present and already begun: our feet have been and are now standing — here we stand at last at thy gates, the pilgrims halting to gaze as they arrive.
Future and near: after seventy years with their hearts in Jerusalem and their feet in Chaldea, they shall shortly stand within the gates.
Spiritual: standing means attendance and continuance at the gates of wisdom, and looks on to the gates of the New Jerusalem.

outliers.summary: Disputes the ancient versions here, holding that the Greek and Latin give the second verb a neuter sense and so vitiate the meaning, and that the Hebrew particle must be resolved into an adverb of time.
Rests the whole verse on the plural: the word was not 'go' but 'let us go', which gave the ear a double joy — for the others' willingness and for their thinking enough of him to ask.

themes: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the Lord.
Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem.
Jerusalem is builded as a city that is compact together:
Whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the Lord, unto the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the Lord.

5.pericope_label: For there are set thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David. Pray for the peace of Jerusalem... Because of the house of the Lord our God I will seek thy good

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes apart the idiom of asking after a city's peace, showing it to be a salutation; Ellicott reads the thrones as evidence about date and points out that the formal Eastern greeting appears in the closing verses.
Gill reads walls, army and brethren all of the church, and insists the closing motive is the sanctuary rather than any private interest.

Clarke hears the alliteration of the Hebrew, sets it beside older English verse, and ends on the civic duty of praying for one's own country; Wesley distinguishes the royal throne from the seats of justice beneath it.
Henry turns the petition into a discipline of prayer, supplying the words, the objects, and the refusal to leave public prayer to the professionals.

debates.question: What does the mention of the thrones of the house of David establish?

positions.summary: That justice was administered in Jerusalem by courts under the Davidic house — and while those thrones stood, the people had justice.
A royal throne allotted to David and his posterity, with inferior seats of justice under his authority, supreme in ecclesiastical and civil affairs alike.
It disposes of the psalm's title but does not prove the monarchy was still standing, since even the later council might administer justice from the throne of David's successors.

debates.question: What is being asked in 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem'?

positions.summary: A salutation. To ask someone's peace is to find out his prosperity by asking and to be animated by the wish that he prosper; in Syriac the same phrase simply means to greet.
Intercession as the appointed way of fetching in mercy, offered from a principle of love rather than custom, and seconded by whatever endeavours lie within our sphere.
Prayer for the church at large rather than for the literal city only — for the coming of the Peacemaker and the peace of his members.
A wish for unanimity and increasing prosperity, in which those who love the city find their own.

outliers.summary: Turns from exegesis to civic polemic: praying for one's country is a duty, and of those who instead raise seditions and subvert its institutions he says that hemp would be disgraced by hanging them.
Reports the Targum's alternative rendering 'in thine army' for 'within thy walls', which makes the petition a wish of success to the church militant.

themes: For there are set thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David.
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee.
Peace be within thy walls, and prosperity within thy palaces.
For my brethren and companions’ sakes, I will now say, Peace be within thee.
Because of the house of the Lord our God I will seek thy good.
